title: Standard-Fractionated Proton Beam Therapy for pediatric diffuse Choroidal Hemangioma in Sturge-Weber Syndrome: A retrospective case series with long-Term follow-Up
summary:
Background: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a rare, non-inherited condition that can affect the skin, brain, and eyes. Some children with this condition develop an abnormal growth of blood vessels in the layer at the back of the eye called the choroid. Fluid leaking from these blood vessels can cause the retina to detach, potentially leading to permanent damage to vision. One treatment option is proton beam therapy, which uses precisely targeted radiation to treat the abnormal blood vessels while aiming to protect the surrounding healthy tissue. However, only limited information is available on the long-term outcomes of this treatment in children with this rare condition.

Research question: The aim of this study is to investigate the long-term effectiveness and safety of proton beam therapy in children with Sturge-Weber syndrome and abnormal blood vessels in the choroid. In particular, the study examines whether the condition remains controlled after treatment and whether further treatment is needed. Changes in vision, pressure inside the eye, the size of the abnormal blood vessel growth, and possible treatment-related side effects are also assessed.

Methods: This retrospective study reviews the medical records of four children who received proton beam therapy because fluid had accumulated beneath the retina. Treatment consisted of ten individual sessions, with a total radiation dose of 20 Gray. Data from examinations performed before treatment and during subsequent follow-up are evaluated retrospectively. The study focuses on whether the condition returns, whether additional treatment is required, changes in vision and pressure inside the eye, changes in the size of the abnormal blood vessel growth, and possible side effects of treatment. The follow-up period ranged from two to four years, depending on the child. As the study includes only four children and has no comparison group, the results are descriptive and are intended to provide further insight into the long-term outcomes of this treatment.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Children with a confirmed diagnosis of Sturge-Weber syndrome.
Presence of unilateral diffuse choroidal hemangioma.
Presence for indicating proton beam therapy.
Treatment with standard-fractionated proton beam therapy at a total dose of 20 Gy delivered in ten fractions of 2.0 Gy each.
Availability of medical records and ophthalmological examination findings before treatment, as well as follow-up data.
Study period: Retrospective review of the medical records of four children who received proton beam therapy at University Hospital Essen. The follow-up period ranged from two to four years after treatment, depending on the patient.
Exclusion criteria:
No confirmed diagnosis of Sturge-Weber syndrome.
Absence of diffuse choroidal hemangioma or bilateral involvement.
No indication for proton beam therapy.
No treatment with standard-fractionated proton beam therapy at a total dose of 20 Gy delivered in ten fractions of 2.0 Gy each.
Insufficient medical records or missing ophthalmological examination and follow-up data required to assess treatment outcomes.
